lessons.title: Proximate Analysis and Beyond: Understanding Feed Composition
lessons.body:
Proximate analysis is the standard lab test that breaks a feed ingredient into six parts: moisture, crude protein, crude fat, crude fibre, ash (minerals), and nitrogen-free extract (NFE, mostly sugars and starches). In Africa, you can send samples to labs like the Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (KALRO) or private labs in Nigeria and South Africa. A basic test costs about $30â$80. For example, maize grain typically has 8â10% crude protein, 3â4% fat, 2% fibre, and 1â2% ash. But proximate analysis does not tell you the quality of the protein or the availability of minerals. That is why we go 'beyond'.

Beyond proximate analysis, you need to know the digestible energy and amino acid profile. For instance, two maize samples can both show 9% protein, but one may have poorly digestible protein due to heat damage. You can request a pepsin digestibility test or an in vitro gas production test to estimate energy. Also, check for anti-nutritional factors like trypsin inhibitors in soybeans or tannins in sorghum. These are not part of proximate analysis but can drastically reduce pig performance.

Practical steps: Collect a representative sample of each ingredient. Use a quartering method to reduce the sample to about 500g. Send it to a reputable lab. Ask for moisture, crude protein, crude fibre, fat, ash, and also calcium and phosphorus. For energy, ask for digestible energy (DE) or metabolisable energy (ME) if available. If not, use published tables like the NRC (2012) or INRA (2004) for African feedstuffs. But remember, local varieties differ. So test at least once per season.

Use the results to adjust your formulation. If your maize has 8% protein instead of 9%, you need to add more soybean meal or another protein source. If your fishmeal has high ash (over 20%), it may be diluted with sand or bone. Reject it. Keep a record of each supplier's analysis. Over time, you will know which suppliers give consistent quality. This simple practice can save you 10â15% on feed costs and improve pig growth by 5â10%.

lessons.title: Energy Evaluation Systems for Pigs: DE, ME, NE
lessons.body:
Energy is the most expensive part of pig feed. To formulate correctly, you need to know how much energy an ingredient provides. There are three systems: Digestible Energy (DE), Metabolisable Energy (ME), and Net Energy (NE). DE is the gross energy of feed minus energy lost in faeces. ME is DE minus energy lost in urine and gases. NE is ME minus energy lost as heat (thermic effect). For pigs, ME is most commonly used in Africa because it is practical and tables are widely available. NE is more accurate for growing pigs and sows but requires more data.

In practice, you will see values like: maize DE = 14.5 MJ/kg, ME = 13.8 MJ/kg; soybean meal DE = 16.5 MJ/kg, ME = 15.5 MJ/kg; wheat bran DE = 10.5 MJ/kg, ME = 9.8 MJ/kg. These numbers come from NRC (2012) or INRA. But local ingredients vary. For example, cassava chips have lower energy (DE ~12 MJ/kg) because of high fibre and moisture. You can estimate DE from proximate analysis using equations: DE (MJ/kg) = 0.0184 Ã crude protein (%) + 0.038 Ã fat (%) + 0.017 Ã NFE (%) â 0.0001 Ã fibre (%). This is a rough guide.

To use these systems, start with a target ME for your pig class. For example, weaners need 14.5 MJ ME/kg, growers 13.5 MJ ME/kg, and sows 12.5 MJ ME/kg. Then calculate the ME contributed by each ingredient. If your mix is low, add more maize or oil. If high, add fibre. Remember, pigs eat to meet energy needs, so if feed is low in energy, they eat more and you spend more. If too high, they may get fat. Balanced energy is key.

Tools: You can use simple Excel spreadsheets or apps like Feed Formulation (available on Google Play) that have built-in ME values. Always check the source of the values. For African conditions, prefer values from tropical feed databases like the FAO's Tropical Feeds or the ILRI feed database. Test your final feed for ME using near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) if available at a local lab. This costs about $20 per sample but can save you money by catching errors before you mix tonnes of feed.

lessons.title: Protein and Amino Acid Digestibility: Ileal vs. Fecal
lessons.body:
Crude protein (CP) on a feed label is not the same as what the pig can use. Pigs need amino acids (AA), the building blocks of protein. The digestibility of protein tells you how much of the CP is absorbed. There are two ways to measure it: faecal digestibility (what disappears before the faeces) and ileal digestibility (what disappears before the end of the small intestine). Ileal is more accurate because microbes in the large intestine can alter protein, giving misleading faecal values. For pigs, ileal digestibility is the gold standard.

In practice, you will see terms like apparent ileal digestibility (AID) and standardised ileal digestibility (SID). SID corrects for endogenous losses (proteins from the pig's own gut). For example, soybean meal has SID lysine of 89%, while maize has 78%. Fishmeal has 92%. These values matter because lysine is the first limiting amino acid in most pig diets. If you formulate based on total CP, you may overfeed or underfeed lysine. For instance, a diet with 18% CP from maize and soybean meal may meet lysine needs, but if you use cassava and cottonseed meal, you may need synthetic lysine.

To apply this, get a feed table with SID AA values. The NRC (2012) and INRA (2004) provide these. For African ingredients, the ILRI feed database has some values. If not available, use AID and adjust. For example, if you use 10% fishmeal (SID lysine 92%) and 20% soybean meal (SID lysine 89%), you can calculate the total SID lysine. Then compare to the pig's requirement: weaners need 1.2% SID lysine, growers 0.9%, sows 0.6%. If short, add synthetic lysine (L-lysine HCl, 78% lysine).

Testing for digestibility is expensive (in vivo trials cost thousands). Instead, use published values and adjust for local processing. Over-heating soybean meal reduces lysine digestibility. So ask your supplier for the processing method. If you suspect poor quality, a simple urease test (for soy) or protein solubility test can indicate over-processing. For other ingredients, use your records: if pigs grow slower than expected on a diet that should meet needs, protein digestibility may be low. Then consider changing the source or adding enzymes like phytase or protease. These can improve digestibility by 5â10%.

lessons.title: Mineral Bioavailability and Interactions
lessons.body:
Minerals are needed in small amounts but are critical for pig health and growth. The total amount in a feed ingredient is not what matters most; it is the bioavailable fractionâthe portion the pig can actually absorb and use. For example, calcium in limestone is highly available (about 90%), but calcium in dicalcium phosphate is about 95%. Phosphorus in plant seeds is mostly bound as phytate, which pigs cannot digest unless phytase is added. So while maize has 0.3% phosphorus, only 0.1% is available. That is why you must formulate on available phosphorus (aP), not total.

Common minerals and their bioavailability: Calcium (limestone, oyster shell) â 90â95%; Phosphorus (monocalcium phosphate) â 95%; Phosphorus (dicalcium phosphate) â 90â95%; Phosphorus (bone meal) â 85â90%; Zinc (zinc sulphate) â 90%; Zinc (zinc oxide) â 50â60%; Copper (copper sulphate) â 80%; Iron (ferrous sulphate) â 80%. In Africa, many small-scale mixers use bone meal or rock phosphate, which may have low availability and heavy metal contamination. Always source from reputable suppliers and ask for a certificate of analysis.

Interactions between minerals can reduce bioavailability. For example, high calcium (above 1.0%) binds with zinc and phosphorus, making them less available. High zinc (above 2000 ppm) can interfere with copper absorption. High iron can reduce zinc and copper uptake. So balance is key. For pigs, the calcium to available phosphorus ratio should be between 1.5:1 and 2:1 for growing pigs, and 2:1 to 2.5:1 for sows. If you use high-calcium ingredients like limestone, you may need to add more zinc and copper.

Practical steps: Use a mineral premix that is specifically for pigs. These premixes contain the right minerals in available forms and correct ratios. If you mix your own, use the following sources: limestone for calcium, monocalcium or dicalcium phosphate for phosphorus, zinc sulphate for zinc, copper sulphate for copper, ferrous sulphate for iron, and potassium iodate for iodine. Add phytase enzyme (500 FTU/kg) to release phytate phosphorus, reducing the need for inorganic phosphorus. This can save $5â$10 per tonne. Always store minerals in a dry place; moisture reduces availability. Test your final feed for calcium and phosphorus at least twice a year to ensure you are meeting requirements without excess.

lessons.title: Anti-Nutritional Factors in Feed Ingredients
lessons.body:
Anti-nutritional factors (ANFs) are natural compounds in feed ingredients that reduce nutrient digestion, absorption, or pig health. Common ANFs in African feedstuffs include trypsin inhibitors in raw soybeans, tannins in sorghum and faba beans, gossypol in cottonseed meal, cyanogenic glycosides in cassava, and phytate in cereals and oilseeds. These can cause poor growth, diarrhoea, or even death if not managed. For example, raw soybeans contain trypsin inhibitor that blocks protein digestion. Pigs fed raw soybeans can lose weight. But proper heating (toasting, extrusion) destroys the inhibitor. A simple urease test can tell if soybeans are properly heated: if urease activity is above 0.2 mg N/g/min, they are under-heated.

Tannins in sorghum bind proteins and reduce digestibility. High-tannin sorghum (above 0.5% tannin) should be avoided or treated with polyethylene glycol or soaked in water. Low-tannin varieties (like white sorghum) are better. Cottonseed meal contains gossypol, which is toxic to pigs. Limit cottonseed meal to 5% of the diet for growing pigs and 0% for breeding pigs. Use only glandless cottonseed varieties if available. Cassava (manioc) contains cyanogenic glycosides, which release cyanide when eaten. Fresh cassava must be sun-dried or soaked for 24 hours to reduce cyanide. Dried cassava chips are safer but still should be limited to 30% of the diet for pigs.

Phytate is another ANF that binds phosphorus, zinc, iron, and calcium. Adding phytase enzyme (500â1000 FTU/kg feed) breaks down phytate, improving mineral availability and reducing environmental pollution. Other ANFs include lectins in beans, saponins in alfalfa, and erucic acid in rapeseed. For beans (like faba beans), heat treatment or soaking reduces lectins. For rapeseed meal, limit to 10% for pigs and use low-erucic acid varieties (canola).

Practical advice: Know the ANFs in your ingredients. Process them correctly. For soybeans, heat until urease activity is below 0.2. For cassava, dry or soak. For cottonseed, limit inclusion. For sorghum, choose low-tannin types. Always test new batches. If you see poor performance, check for ANFs. Simple on-farm tests like the urease test for soy and the picrate test for cyanide in cassava can be done with kits from agricultural suppliers. These cost $10â$20 and can save you from a bad batch.

lessons.title: Ingredient Quality Control and Purchasing Specifications
lessons.body:
Quality control (QC) ensures you get what you pay for. Without QC, you may buy maize with 15% moisture (which molds) or fishmeal mixed with sand. In Africa, where feed fraud is common, QC is essential. Start with a purchasing specification: a written document that states the minimum requirements for each ingredient. For example, for maize: moisture max 13%, crude protein min 8%, aflatoxin max 20 ppb, foreign matter max 2%, and no live insects. For soybean meal: moisture max 12%, crude protein min 44%, urease activity max 0.2, and fibre max 7%. For fishmeal: moisture max 10%, crude protein min 60%, ash max 20%, and salt max 3%. Give this spec to your supplier and make it part of the contract.

When you receive a delivery, inspect it. Take a representative sample using a spear or by hand from at least 10 random bags. Check for colour, smell, and texture. Moldy smell means aflatoxin risk. For maize, look for broken kernels and dust. For fishmeal, smell for freshnessârancid fishmeal has oxidized fats. Use simple tools: a moisture meter (cost $50â$100) to check moisture on the spot. A sieve to check foreign matter. A magnet to check for metal pieces. For aflatoxin, use a rapid test kit (like ELISA) that costs $5â$10 per sample. If aflatoxin is above 20 ppb, reject the load.

Keep records. For each delivery, record supplier, date, quantity, and test results. Over time, you will see which suppliers are reliable. Consider forming a buying group with other farmers to negotiate better prices and demand quality. In many African countries, the bureau of standards (like KEBS in Kenya, SON in Nigeria) has feed ingredient standards. Use them as a reference. Also, ask for a certificate of analysis (COA) from the supplier. But do not trust it blindlyâverify with your own tests.

If you cannot test everything, prioritize: moisture, crude protein, and aflatoxin for maize; urease and protein for soybean meal; protein and ash for fishmeal. For other ingredients, check for adulteration. For example, groundnut meal may be mixed with sand. A simple sedimentation test in water can reveal sand. Remember, QC costs money but saves more. A batch of aflatoxin-contaminated maize can kill your pigs. A load of low-protein soybean meal can slow growth for weeks. So invest in a moisture meter, aflatoxin test kits, and a good relationship with a reliable lab. This is the foundation of profitable pig farming.

quiz.q: What does proximate analysis measure?
options: B) Moisture, crude protein, fat, fibre, ash, NFE
quiz.explanation: Proximate analysis is the standard six-part test for moisture, protein, fat, fibre, ash, and nitrogen-free extract.

quiz.q: Which lab test can indicate if soybean meal is under-heated?
quiz.explanation: The urease test measures urease activity, which is high in under-heated soybeans and should be below 0.2 mg N/g/min.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between DE and ME?
options: A) ME includes urine and gas losses
C) ME is only for sows
quiz.explanation: Metabolisable energy (ME) is digestible energy (DE) minus energy lost in urine and gases.

quiz.q: Which energy system is most commonly used in pig feed formulation in Africa?
quiz.explanation: ME is practical and widely available in feed tables, making it the most common system used in Africa.

quiz.q: Why is ileal digestibility preferred over faecal digestibility for pigs?
options: B) It avoids microbial alteration in the large intestine
quiz.explanation: Ileal digestibility measures absorption before the large intestine, where microbes can alter protein, giving misleading faecal values.

quiz.q: What does SID stand for in protein digestibility?
quiz.explanation: SID corrects for endogenous losses, giving a more accurate measure of amino acid availability.

quiz.q: Which amino acid is typically first limiting in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: Lysine is the first limiting amino acid in most cereal-based pig diets.

quiz.q: What is the bioavailability of phosphorus in maize?
quiz.explanation: Most phosphorus in maize is bound as phytate, so only about 30% is available without phytase.

quiz.q: Which mineral interaction can reduce zinc availability?
quiz.explanation: High calcium binds with zinc, making it less available for absorption.

quiz.q: What is the recommended calcium to available phosphorus ratio for growing pigs?
quiz.explanation: A ratio of 1.5:1 to 2:1 is optimal for growing pigs to avoid mineral interactions.

quiz.q: Which enzyme can be added to pig feed to improve phosphorus availability?
quiz.explanation: Phytase breaks down phytate, releasing bound phosphorus and other minerals.

quiz.q: What is an anti-nutritional factor in raw soybeans?
quiz.explanation: Trypsin inhibitors block protein digestion and are destroyed by proper heating.

quiz.q: How can you reduce cyanide in cassava for pig feed?
quiz.explanation: Sun-drying or soaking for 24 hours reduces cyanogenic glycosides in cassava.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended inclusion of cottonseed meal for growing pigs?
quiz.explanation: Cottonseed meal contains gossypol, which is toxic, so limit to 5% for growing pigs.

quiz.q: Which test can detect aflatoxin in maize?
quiz.explanation: ELISA is a rapid test for aflatoxin and is commonly used on farms.

quiz.q: What is a purchasing specification?
options: B) A written document with minimum quality requirements
quiz.explanation: A purchasing spec states the minimum requirements for each ingredient, such as moisture and protein content.

quiz.q: What is the maximum moisture content for safe storage of maize?
quiz.explanation: Maize with more than 13% moisture is prone to mold and aflatoxin production.

quiz.q: Which tool can check moisture on the spot?
quiz.explanation: A moisture meter gives instant readings and costs about $50â$100.

quiz.q: What does a certificate of analysis (COA) provide?
options: B) Test results for a batch
quiz.explanation: A COA shows the test results for a specific batch of ingredient.

quiz.q: Why is it important to take a representative sample?
options: B) To ensure test results reflect the whole batch
quiz.explanation: A representative sample ensures that lab results are accurate for the entire lot.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of poor-quality fishmeal?
quiz.explanation: Rancid smell indicates oxidized fats, meaning poor quality or old fishmeal.

quiz.q: What is the typical crude protein content of good-quality soybean meal?
quiz.explanation: Soybean meal should have at least 44% crude protein.

quiz.q: What is the recommended maximum inclusion of high-tannin sorghum in pig diets?
quiz.explanation: High-tannin sorghum should be avoided; use low-tannin varieties instead.

quiz.q: Which mineral source has the highest phosphorus bioavailability?
quiz.explanation: Monocalcium phosphate has about 95% phosphorus bioavailability.

quiz.q: What is the main role of phytase in pig feed?
quiz.explanation: Phytase breaks down phytate to release phosphorus, improving mineral availability.

quiz.q: Which feed ingredient is most likely to contain gossypol?
quiz.explanation: Gossypol is a toxic compound found in cottonseed meal.

quiz.q: What is the first step in quality control when receiving a delivery?
quiz.explanation: Inspect and take a representative sample before accepting the delivery.

quiz.q: Which of these is a simple on-farm test for sand in groundnut meal?
quiz.explanation: Sand sinks in water, so sedimentation can reveal adulteration.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended level of aflatoxin in maize for pig feed?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin above 20 ppb is unsafe for pigs and should be rejected.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of supplier test results?
quiz.explanation: Records help you track which suppliers consistently provide quality ingredients.
